themes.name: Accidental breaking changes in JavaScript/TypeScript library releases
themes.description: Library releases labelled minor or patch that nonetheless break downstream code, and whether a small open-source tool could catch them before publishing.
themes.notes: Chosen by the owner from three VENTURE-proposed candidates, with an explicit practical-value bar: ideas should be buildable, open-sourceable tools.

problems.title: Minor and patch releases break dependents' code
problems.statement: Package managers install minor and patch updates automatically on the promise that they're backward compatible. When a library breaks that promise, downstream projects break without warning. Users report pinned versions, broken release pipelines and lost weekends.
problems.affectedUsers: Developers and teams depending on npm packages, and maintainers of libraries built on other libraries
problems.severityNote: High when it happens: broken builds and pipelines, and emergency pinning.
problems.frequencyNote: Hundreds of GitHub issues are titled about it. True frequency not yet measured.

problems.title: Existing semver checkers only see the type surface
problems.statement: The available and emerging checkers compare TypeScript type declarations. Many real breaking releases come from behaviour changes or from package metadata (e.g. a raised Node engine requirement), which those tools don't inspect.
problems.affectedUsers: Maintainers relying on automated checks, and especially packages without TypeScript types
problems.severityNote: Medium: a gap in tooling, not a direct harm.
problems.frequencyNote: All four real complaints examined were non-type breaks (small sample).

competitors.name: cargo-semver-checks (Rust)
competitors.description: Rust's established semver linter with a GitHub Action. It checks a crate's public API before publishing. About 1,700 GitHub stars at retrieval.

competitors.name: Microsoft API Extractor
competitors.description: A TypeScript tool that snapshots a library's public API (.d.ts) so changes can be reviewed, among several other jobs (doc generation, .d.ts rollups).
weaknesses: Heavy setup aimed at larger teams (inference)

competitors.name: New TypeScript semver checkers (Clerk break-check, ts-semver-checks, semver-check)
competitors.description: Several 2026 projects that diff the exported TypeScript surface between versions and fail CI on an insufficient version bump. Clerk's is company-backed and uses API Extractor plus an AI review.
weaknesses: Very new; little adoption (0–3 stars at retrieval)
Type surface only: blind to engines, exports and other metadata breaks

ideas.title: TypeScript API-surface semver checker
ideas.summary: A 'cargo-semver-checks for TypeScript': diff the exported .d.ts surface between the last release and the next, and fail CI if the version bump understates the change.
ideas.targetUsers: Maintainers of TypeScript libraries on npm
ideas.solution: Generate API snapshots from .d.ts files, classify each change as major, minor or patch, and compare with the planned version bump in a CLI and GitHub Action.
ideas.differentiation: None that's clear: at least three 2026 projects and Microsoft's API Extractor already do this.
ideas.feasibility: Feasible: the TypeScript compiler API exposes the surface.

assumptions.text: Most accidental breaking releases are type-surface changes

objections.text: Already being built by at least three projects, one company-backed (Clerk), on top of Microsoft's API Extractor.
None of the four real breakage complaints examined (React, node-abort-controller, floating-ui, polished) was a type-surface change, so the approach misses many real breaks.

severity.rationale: Breaking minor releases cost users real time (weekends, pinned versions).

frequency.rationale: Hundreds of issues titled about it; true frequency not yet measured.

ideas.statusRationale: Rejected. The TypeScript type-surface checker niche is already being filled (Clerk's break-check, ts-semver-checks, semver-check, API Extractor), and the real complaints examined weren't type-surface breaks.

practical.smallestUsefulVersion: A CLI and GitHub Action that diffs .d.ts exports between versions.
practical.buildNote: Straightforward with the TypeScript compiler API.
practical.monetization: Unlikely: several free tools already exist.

ideas.title: Release-contract linter for npm packages
ideas.summary: Before publishing, check the parts of a release's contract that type checkers ignore: engine requirements tightened, entry points or exports paths removed, module format switched, new required peer dependencies, removed CLI commands. Fail if a minor or patch release changes them.
ideas.targetUsers: Maintainers of JavaScript and TypeScript packages on npm (including packages without types)
ideas.solution: A CLI and GitHub Action that compares the package.json and published file list of the release candidate with the last published version on npm, and flags contract changes that need a major bump (engines.node raised, exports subpaths removed or an exports map added, main/module/types removed, type: module switch, new non-optional peer dependencies, bin entries removed). It can run alongside a type-surface checker.
ideas.differentiation: Existing tools inspect the TypeScript type surface. This inspects the install- and import-time contract, which breaks even for untyped packages (e.g. polished's engines bump). It complements the type checkers rather than replacing them.
ideas.feasibility: High. Everything needed is in package.json and the npm registry metadata. No compiler work is needed.

assumptions.text: Metadata-level contract breaks in minor or patch releases are common among popular packages (≥ 20% shipped at least one in two years)
Flags are mostly genuine breaks rather than noise (≥ 70% of audited flags)
Maintainers would add another check to their release workflow

risks: The rules may be too strict (some engines bumps are deliberate and announced)
Existing checkers may add metadata rules
nextSteps: If supported, build the CLI and dogfood it on real packages

objections.text: Behaviour changes, like React 16.4's, are invisible to any static check, so this catches only part of the problem.
objections.response: It doesn't need to catch everything to be useful. The experiment measures how much it catches.

objections.text: Some maintainers deliberately tighten engines in minor releases (e.g. dropping end-of-life Node). They may consider that acceptable, and see the linter as noise.
objections.response: The audit step measures how many flags are genuine. Rules can be configured.

objections.text: The type-checker projects could add metadata rules quickly.

severity.rationale: Breaking minor releases cost users real time.

frequency.rationale: Frequency of metadata breaks unknown; being measured.

userValue.rationale: Catches a class of breaks no current tool checks, before publish.

competitiveGap.rationale: No tool found that checks the install/import contract.

userAccess.rationale: Maintainers reachable via GitHub Marketplace and npm.

validationCost.rationale: Frequency testable for $0 on registry data.

ideas.statusRationale: Advanced. It covers breaks that the existing TypeScript checkers can't see, is cheap to build, and VENTURE can measure how often such breaks happen directly from npm before building anything.
ideas.noveltyNote: Distinct from the rejected type-surface checker: it inspects package metadata and the published file contract, not .d.ts types.

practical.adopters: npm package maintainers, as a pre-publish check, and possibly downstream teams auditing updates
practical.smallestUsefulVersion: A CLI (`npx`) and GitHub Action that compares the release candidate's package.json and file list with the last published version and prints contract changes needing a major bump.
practical.buildNote: Needs only package.json parsing, npm registry metadata and the semver library. VENTURE already uses all three.
practical.monetization: As a free open-source tool. A paid angle (dependency-update risk scoring for companies) is speculative.

ideas.title: Downstream dependent test runner ('crater for npm')
ideas.summary: Before releasing, run the test suites of a sample of the package's dependents against the release candidate, to catch behaviour breaks that static checks miss.
ideas.targetUsers: Maintainers of widely used npm packages
ideas.solution: A service that picks dependents with test suites, installs the release candidate in their place, runs their tests, and reports regressions.
ideas.differentiation: Catches behaviour breaks like React 16.4's, which no static tool can.
ideas.feasibility: Hard: arbitrary test suites need sandboxed execution, and the compute cost is significant.

assumptions.text: Enough dependents have runnable test suites

objections.text: Running thousands of untrusted test suites safely is expensive and complex. It's not something VENTURE can build or run for free.

severity.rationale: Behaviour breaks are the hardest to catch.

competitiveGap.rationale: Not found for npm; not searched exhaustively.

ideas.statusRationale: Parked. Potentially valuable, but expensive and risky to run (executing untrusted code at scale), and well beyond what VENTURE can build for free.

practical.smallestUsefulVersion: A GitHub Action that runs the tests of 10 hand-picked dependents against a release candidate.
practical.buildNote: Needs sandboxed execution of untrusted code and paid compute.
practical.monetization: Possible as a hosted service for large maintainers or companies, but costly to operate.

ideas.title: Publish-anomaly alarm for maintainers
ideas.summary: Watches the registry for new versions of a maintainer's own packages and alerts within minutes if a release differs structurally from the maintainer's normal releases.
ideas.targetUsers: Maintainers of widely used packages without a security team
ideas.solution: Subscribe to registry publish events for owned packages. Diff each release against the previous one for structural anomalies: newly added dependencies, new install-time hooks or .pth files, publishing outside the usual CI identity, missing provenance. Notify the maintainer through an out-of-band channel they control.
ideas.differentiation: Maintainer-side and owner-verified: the maintainer can say 'that wasn't me' fastest. Vendors protect consumers after analysis.
ideas.feasibility: Registry metadata and tarballs are public. The anomaly rules are simple diffs.

assumptions.text: Malicious releases from compromised accounts differ structurally (new deps, new hooks, different publisher) from the maintainer's normal releases
Maintainers would notice and react faster than the current detection time (~3 h for axios)
Commercial scanners don't already offer free maintainer-side alerts
A substantial share of popular packages still publish in a way a stolen token could reproduce (no trusted publishing, no staged approval)

risks: An attacker who controls the account may also control the notification channel
Vendors may already cover this (not examined)
False positives on legitimate dependency changes
nextSteps: If the gap is real, consider a review aid for staged releases that highlights new install hooks at approval time

objections.text: Commercial scanners (Socket, StepSecurity) already analyse new releases quickly. The marginal value of maintainer-side alerts is unproven.
If the attacker controls the maintainer's account or email, alerts may be intercepted.
objections.response: Use a channel registered independently of the registry account.

objections.text: Some attacks, like asyncapi's branch-token compromise, publish through the normal CI pipeline, so publisher-identity checks wouldn't fire.

npm now offers prevention to maintainers who opt in (staged publishing with 2FA approval, token-free publishing), and PyPI warns about token uploads to trusted-publishing projects. The alarm only adds value for maintainers who haven't adopted these.
objections.response: Measure adoption: if most popular packages still publish without these protections, the alarm's audience remains large (exp-npm-publishing-practices).

severity.rationale: RATs and credential stealers in packages with huge reach.

frequency.rationale: Several high-profile incidents in 2026 in the captured signals.

userValue.rationale: Could cut exposure windows, if anomalies are detectable.

competitiveGap.rationale: Vendors exist; maintainer-side free alerts not verified either way.

validationCost.rationale: Can be checked retrospectively on public registry data for $0.

ideas.statusRationale: Stays advanced. The technical premise (most hijacks add install hooks) and the audience (about half of popular packages still publish without npm's new protections, including most previously hijacked ones) are both supported by pre-registered experiments. Remaining unknowns: whether maintainers want such alerts and act on them, and whether vendors already offer them.

practical.adopters: Maintainers of npm packages, especially those not using trusted publishing or staged approval (about half of popular packages)
practical.smallestUsefulVersion: A GitHub Action or small service that watches your own packages on npm and alerts you when a new release adds an install script or an unexpected dependency.
practical.buildNote: The same registry diffing VENTURE already runs daily in the install-hook watch.
practical.monetization: Mainly as a free open-source tool. Security vendors and npm itself are moving into this space, so a paid product is unlikely.

experiments.title: How often do popular npm packages ship metadata-level breaking changes in minor or patch releases?
experiments.hypothesis: At least 20% of popular npm packages shipped at least one minor or patch release in the past 24 months that a release-contract linter would flag. At least 70% of a random sample of flags are genuine breaking changes.
experiments.uncertainty: Whether the problem the linter targets is common enough (assumption a1), and whether its flags would be trusted (assumption a2).
procedure: Pre-registered 2026-11-04 before any release data was collected.
Population: the 400 popular npm packages from exp-npm-publishing-practices.
For each package, take consecutive non-prerelease versions published in the 24 months before 2026-11-04, keeping pairs where the later one is a minor or patch bump of the earlier.

Rules (from registry metadata): engines.node minimum raised; exports subpath removed, or an exports map added where none existed; main, module, types or typings removed; type switched to module; a new non-optional peer dependency added, or an existing peer's minimum major raised; a bin entry removed.
Report the share of packages with at least one flagged release, the share of release pairs flagged, and counts per rule.
Audit: a research session reviews 20 randomly sampled flags (fixed seed) and judges each as a genuine break per SemVer or not, documenting reasons.
successCriteria: At least 20% of packages have at least one flagged minor or patch release in the window, and at least 70% of the 20 audited flags are genuine breaks
failureCriteria: Fewer than 5% of packages have a flagged release (the problem is too rare to justify a tool)
Fewer than 50% of audited flags are genuine (too noisy)
experiments.estimatedTime: < 1 hour of automated analysis plus a manual audit of 20 flags
experiments.expectedLearning: Whether a release-contract linter would catch a meaningful number of real breaks with acceptable noise, before anything is built.

nextSteps.ifSuccess: Build the CLI and GitHub Action, and dogfood it by running it over recent releases of popular packages.
nextSteps.ifFailure: Reject or narrow the idea to the rules that proved common and precise.

briefs.researchQuestion: Libraries regularly ship 'minor' or 'patch' updates that break the code of everyone using them, even though those updates are installed automatically on the promise of being safe. Could a small open-source tool catch these breaks before a release is published?
briefs.whyItMatters: Every JavaScript project depends on dozens to hundreds of packages and trusts version numbers to signal risk. When a minor release breaks that trust, users lose time pinning versions and debugging, and maintainers lose credibility. Rust has a widely adopted tool for this; JavaScript has no established equivalent.
subQuestions: How often do popular npm packages ship breaking changes in minor or patch releases?
What kinds of breaks are they: type changes, behaviour changes, or metadata changes?
What do existing and emerging tools catch, and what do they miss?
Is there a small, buildable tool that catches a meaningful share with little noise?

findings.statement: Breaking minor and patch releases cost users real time. Reports describe whole codebases breaking after a React minor update, release pipelines broken for a weekend, and maintainers forced to pin versions. Microsoft built API Extractor partly because users 'keep reporting that their code won't compile after a supposedly minor update'.
findings.strength: Moderate. Several independent reports plus Microsoft's own stated motivation. Individual cases, not a measured rate.

findings.statement: The tool model works elsewhere: Rust's cargo-semver-checks (about 1,700 stars, with a GitHub Action) checks releases for semver violations, though it documents breaks it can't catch.
findings.strength: Strong as evidence that a tool exists and is adopted in Rust. It doesn't show JS maintainers would adopt one.

findings.statement: The TypeScript type-surface checker niche is filling up: Clerk's break-check (company-backed), ts-semver-checks and semver-check all appeared in 2026, alongside Microsoft's API Extractor.
findings.strength: Strong for existence. All are very new, with little adoption yet.

findings.statement: Type checkers miss many real breaks. None of the four complaints examined was a type change: they were behaviour changes (React, floating-ui, node-abort-controller) and a metadata change (polished raised its required Node version in a minor release).
findings.strength: Weak to moderate. A small sample, but it points to a clear gap: the install and import contract in package metadata.

uncertainties: How often metadata-level breaks actually happen in popular packages (being measured).
Whether maintainers consider deliberate engine bumps in minor releases acceptable.
The four complaints were chosen by GitHub search ranking, not sampled randomly.

conclusion.belief: Accidental breaking releases are a real, recurring cost, and the tool model is proven in Rust. But the obvious product, a TypeScript type-surface checker, is already being built by several projects including a company-backed one. The more promising gap is a release-contract linter that checks what type checkers ignore: engine requirements, entry points and exports, module format, peer dependencies and CLI commands.
conclusion.confidenceReason: Based on one research session: qualitative evidence and a small sample of complaints. How often metadata breaks happen hasn't been measured yet.
unknowns: How many flags would be genuine
Whether maintainers would adopt another release check
conclusion.continueReason: A $0 measurement on npm registry data can show whether the linter would catch enough to be worth building.

nextSteps.text: Measure how often 400 popular npm packages shipped metadata-level breaking changes in minor or patch releases over two years, and audit 20 flags by hand.
If the measurement supports it, build the release-contract linter as an open-source CLI and GitHub Action.
